title: Teaching Coding Agents to do Spreadsheets - Nuno Campos, Witan Labs
talk_summary: Nuno Campos describes four months of work getting coding agents to handle spreadsheets, moving from 50% to 92% on an internal benchmark. The biggest wins came from replacing many tools with a persistent REPL, building high-fidelity verification loops, using deterministic evals where possible, and treating many apparent reasoning failures as plumbing bugs.

takeaways.what_they_do: They replaced about 15 separate spreadsheet tools with one sandboxed Node.js REPL exposing functions, keeping variables/state across calls so the agent can combine operations and interleave reasoning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: with a single a single tool, which was a Node.js REPL
takeaways.numbers: 50% before REPL, 74% after, eventually 92%; zero timeouts under a 5-minute limit

takeaways.what_they_do: They built formula and render engines so the agent could compute/render spreadsheet edits and verify output, iterating until correct; incomplete engines made results worse.
takeaways.numbers: Overall benchmark moved from 50% to 92%; zero timeouts after the REPL/verification approach

takeaways.what_they_do: They replaced LLM-as-judge where possible with golden input/output fixtures, e.g. feed the same inputs into the model-produced spreadsheet and compare outputs to the golden spreadsheet.
takeaways.evidence_quote: replace it with deterministic comparisons wherever that was possible

takeaways.what_they_do: They inspect agent traces to separate model reasoning failures from tool bugs, bad prompt examples, and retry loops.
takeaways.evidence_quote: always check your traces and your plumbing because sometimes agent confusion is just bugs

takeaways.what_they_do: They add domain knowledge to prompts to focus the model on relevant terms and criteria; it survived tool iterations and improved results.
takeaways.evidence_quote: adding domain knowledge to the prompts

takeaways.technique: Lightweight revisitable plan, not rigid agent split
takeaways.what_they_do: A five-step plan/execute/verify process moved errors earlier, but splitting discovery/execution across agents was too rigid because discovery ran once and context did not flow.
takeaways.evidence_quote: architecture in the end was too rigid
